questions.text: Write the equation for the equilibrium occurring in a saturated solution of silver chloride, AgCl.

Calculate the solubility of AgCl in water at 25 degrees C, and give [Ag+] and [Cl-].

Ks(AgCl) = 1.77 x 10^-10
questions.expectedAnswer: Let solubility be s. [Ag+] = s and [Cl-] = s (1:1 ratio). Ks = s x s = s^2. s = sqrt(1.77 x 10^-10) = 1.33 x 10^-5 mol L-1. So [Ag+] = [Cl-] = 1.33 x 10^-5 mol L-1.
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Achievement:
- Correct process.

For Merit:
- Correct solubility with units.

questions.text:
Below is a list of solutions available to add to a saturated solution of AgCl:

HCl(aq), NaBr(aq), NH3(aq), KNO3(aq)

Select and justify an appropriate solution to increase the solubility of AgCl.
questions.expectedAnswer: Add NH3. Ammonia forms a complex ion with Ag+, removing Ag+ from the equilibrium and shifting it forward, dissolving more AgCl.
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Achievement:
- Recognises Ag+ can form a complex ion.

For Merit:
- Explains removal of Ag+ from equilibrium.

For Excellence:
- Full justification with equation.

questions.text: Select and justify an appropriate solution to decrease the solubility of AgCl.
questions.expectedAnswer: Add NaCl. Cl- is a common ion; increasing [Cl-] shifts equilibrium to the left (reverse), precipitating more AgCl.
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Achievement:
- Recognises common ion.

For Merit:
- Explains shift to reverse.

questions.text:
Predict, by calculation, whether a precipitate of silver chloride, AgCl, will form when 30.0 mL of 0.0150 mol L-1 silver nitrate, AgNO3, is added to 20.0 mL of 0.0250 mol L-1 sodium chloride, NaCl.

Ks(AgCl) = 1.77 x 10^-10
questions.expectedAnswer: Total volume = 30.0 + 20.0 = 50.0 mL. [Ag+] after mixing = (30.0/50.0) x 0.0150 = 9.00 x 10^-3 mol L-1. [Cl-] after mixing = (20.0/50.0) x 0.0250 = 1.00 x 10^-2 mol L-1. IP = [Ag+][Cl-] = 9.00 x 10^-3 x 1.00 x 10^-2 = 9.00 x 10^-5. IP (9.00 x 10^-5) is much greater than Ks (1.77 x 10^-10), so a precipitate of AgCl will form.
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Achievement:
- Correct [Ag+] OR [Cl-].

For Merit:
- Correct process for IP.

For Excellence:
- Correct calculation and comparison.

questions.text:
List all the species present in a solution of sodium ethanoate, CH3COONa, in order of decreasing concentration. Do not include water.

Na+ > ___ > ___ = ___ > OH- > ___

Sodium ethanoate can be mixed with ethanoic acid, CH3COOH, to form a buffer solution.

Explain how this buffer solution would react upon the addition of a small volume of hydrochloric acid, HCl, including a balanced equation.
questions.expectedAnswer: When HCl is added, the basic component CH3COO- reacts with H3O+ to form CH3COOH, minimising pH change. CH3COO- + H3O+ -> CH3COOH + H2O

WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Achievement:

For Merit:
- Explains the reaction with equation.

questions.text:
Three colourless 0.150 mol L-1 solutions of CH3NH2, CH3COOH, and (CH3NH3)Cl have lost their labels. The solutions are randomly labelled A, B, and C. The electrical conductivity and indicator colour for each solution are shown in the table above.

Identify the three solutions. Justify your identification in terms of degree of dissociation and relative concentration of ions.

graph.title: Unknown Solutions — Conductivity and Indicator Tests

questions.expectedAnswer: A = CH3COOH (weak acid, poor conductivity, yellow = acidic). B = CH3NH2 (weak base, poor conductivity, blue = basic). C = (CH3NH3)Cl (fully dissociates, good conductivity, yellow = acidic salt).
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Achievement:
- Recognises ions needed for conductivity.

For Merit:
- Links conductivity and colour for TWO solutions.

For Excellence:

Ka(CH3COOH) = 1.34 x 10^-5   pKa = 4.87

questions.text:

Consider the initial pH, the pH after 10.0 mL of NaOH has been added, and the shape of the curve.

questions.text:
After a certain volume of NaOH has been added, the CH3COOH and CH3COONa are present in a 1:7 ratio.

Calculate the pH of this solution, and evaluate its buffering ability.
questions.expectedAnswer: pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]) = 4.87 + log(7/1) = 4.87 + 0.845 = 5.72. The buffer is more effective at neutralising added strong acid than added strong base, because there is much more conjugate base (7 parts) than weak acid (1 part) — the conjugate base is available in excess to react with added H+.
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Achievement:
- Correct process.

For Merit:
- Correct pH and explanation.

For Excellence:
- pH and evaluation of buffer effectiveness.

questions.text:
Justify why the pH increases rapidly between 16.0 mL and 20.0 mL (around the equivalence point at 18.0 mL).
No calculations are necessary.
questions.expectedAnswer: As the titration nears 18.0 mL (the equivalence point), the remaining weak acid is almost entirely converted to its conjugate base, so the buffering capacity is depleted and any added OH- has a much larger effect on pH. Just past the equivalence point, excess NaOH is added directly to the solution (no more weak acid to neutralise it), causing the pH to rise very rapidly over this small volume range.
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Achievement:
- Recognises the buffer is no longer effective.

For Merit:
- Explains the rapid pH increase near and past equivalence.

questions.text: Calculate the pH at the equivalence point.
questions.expectedAnswer: At equivalence, all CH3COOH has been converted to CH3COO-. The ethanoate ion hydrolyses: CH3COO- + H2O <=> CH3COOH + OH-. Kb = Kw/Ka = 1 x 10^-14 / 1.34 x 10^-5 = 7.46 x 10^-10. The resulting pH will be basic (around 8-9).
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Achievement:
- Correct process.

For Merit:
- Calculates pH but may not dilute correctly.

For Excellence:
- Correct pH at equivalence.

questions.text:
In a second titration, 20.0 mL of 0.180 mol L-1 methanoic acid, HCOOH, is titrated with the same 0.200 mol L-1 NaOH solution.

Ka(HCOOH) = 1.77 x 10^-4   pKa = 3.75

Predict how the pH at the equivalence point will compare to the first titration with ethanoic acid.

    Lower pH        Same pH        Higher pH

Explain your choice.
questions.expectedAnswer: Lower pH. Methanoic acid has a larger Ka (1.77 x 10^-4) than ethanoic acid (1.34 x 10^-5), so methanoic acid is the stronger of the two weak acids. Its conjugate base (methanoate, HCOO-) is correspondingly a weaker base than ethanoate (CH3COO-). At the equivalence point, the conjugate base hydrolyses in water to produce OH-. Because methanoate is the weaker base, it hydrolyses less, producing a lower [OH-] and therefore a lower pH than the equivalence point of the ethanoic acid titration.
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Achievement:
- Recognises relative acid strengths.

For Merit:
- Links Ka to [OH-] at equivalence.

For Excellence:
- Correct prediction with full explanation.
